TOP OF CASE (10/25/26)
1. Resolutional analysis.
a. The resolution: The United States federal government should prohibit factory farming.
b. This is a policy round because of an actor and the word 'should,' so the criterion is net benefits.
2. Definitions and topicality.

a. 'Concentrated animal feeding operation,' or CAFO, uses the EPA Clean Water Act definition: any facility confining animals for 45+ days in a 12-month period in an area without vegetation at or above EPA head-count thresholds—1,000 beef cattle, 700 dairy cows, 2,500 hogs over 55 lbs, or 125,000 broiler chickens—or discharging pollutants into US waters.
b. Prohibiting CAFOs is directly topical because high-density industrial confinement is the exact production model 'factory farming' describes.
3. Inherency.

a. Under current Clean Water Act rules, the EPA allows most CAFOs to self-certify that they do not discharge into navigable waters, leaving the majority of facilities operating without federal permits.
b. Meatpacking conglomerates like Tyson, JBS, and Smithfield lock contract growers into high-density confinement while federal programs subsidize industrial feed.
PLAN TEXT
The USfg should prohibit concentrated animal feeding operations in the United States.
ADVANTAGE 1: PANDEMICS (10/25/26)
A. Uniqueness
1. Bird flu is already circulating in United States livestock.

a. According to the CDC in 2024, highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza was confirmed in US dairy cattle for the first time in March 2024 and spread across herds in more than a dozen states, infecting dozens of dairy and poultry workers.
b. According to the CDC in January 2025, a patient in Louisiana became the first person in the United States to die from H5N1 infection.
2. Federal surveillance lags behind industrial spread.

a. According to the USDA in December 2024, dairy herd testing started out voluntary and limited, and mandatory national milk testing was delayed for months after the outbreak began, guaranteeing continued mammalian spillover.
3. The brink is human-to-human mutation.
a. Every additional mammalian infection gives the virus another evolutionary opportunity to acquire the receptor mutations required for sustained human-to-human transmission.
B. Link
1. CAFOs are the primary evolutionary incubator for novel influenza.

a. According to the Pew Commission on Industrial Farm Animal Production in 2008, packing thousands of genetically uniform, immunosuppressed animals nose-to-nose in enclosed barns creates the ideal environment for rapid viral amplification and mutation.
2. The plan eliminates the highest-density viral reservoirs.
a. Prohibiting CAFOs shuts down the massive indoor herd and flock concentrations where mild strains mutate into highly pathogenic variants.
C. Internal Link
Prohibiting CAFOs stops zoonotic pandemic emergence in three independent ways:
1. Stopping interspecies mixing is key to preventing viral reassortment.

a. According to the CDC in 2010, pigs carry respiratory receptors for both avian and human influenza strains, acting as genetic mixing vessels—the exact pathway that produced the 2009 H1N1 swine flu pandemic.
2. Lowering herd density is key to cutting viral load.
a. One infected bird in a small flock exposes only that flock, whereas one infected bird in a CAFO barn of 125,000 broilers generates billions of viral copies through continuous serial passage.
3. Eliminating confinement barns is key to severing the worker-to-community bridge.
a. CAFO workers labor in aerosolized waste and often lack paid sick leave, forcing them to work while symptomatic and carry novel strains into surrounding communities.
b. Stopping CAFO amplification prevents both mass pandemic mortality and structural health-system collapse.
D. Impact
1. A human-transmissible H5N1 pandemic causes catastrophic global mortality.

a. According to the World Health Organization in 2024, roughly half of all reported human H5N1 cases worldwide since 2003 have been fatal; even a fraction of that fatality rate in a human pandemic would dwarf COVID-19.
2. Structural hospital and supply-chain collapse.

a. According to the CDC in 2024, COVID-19 killed more than 1.1 million Americans, overwhelmed intensive-care capacity, and triggered multi-trillion-dollar economic disruptions that hit low-income workers hardest.
ADVANTAGE 2: ANTIMICROBIAL RESISTANCE (10/25/26)
A. Uniqueness
1. Antibiotic-resistant superbugs already kill tens of thousands of Americans.
a. According to the CDC in 2019, antibiotic-resistant bacteria and fungi cause more than 2.8 million infections and more than 35,000 direct deaths in the United States every year.
2. Industrial livestock production consumes massive volumes of human-class antibiotics.

a. According to the FDA in 2022, millions of kilograms of medically important antimicrobials—including tetracyclines, penicillins, and macrolides needed in human hospitals—are sold annually for use in food-producing animals.
3. The clinical antibiotic pipeline is exhausted.
a. Few new classes of antibiotics have been discovered in decades, so every drug class lost to agricultural resistance cannot be replaced.
B. Link
1. High-density CAFO confinement requires routine herd-wide medication.

a. Because CAFOs crowd thousands of stressed animals into unhygienic stalls and litter, operators administer antibiotics across entire herds and flocks via feed and water for routine disease prevention.
2. Ending industrial confinement slashes agricultural antibiotic use.

a. According to Aarestrup in 2012, in Nature, after Denmark restricted routine preventative antimicrobial use and reformed swine confinement, antimicrobial use per kilogram of pork fell by more than half while total pig production grew.
C. Internal Link
Banning CAFOs preserves working antibiotics in two independent ways:
1. Removing herd-wide prophylaxis is key to halting evolutionary selection pressure.
a. Continuous low-dose medication across thousands of confined animals kills susceptible bacteria and selects for resistant superbugs that multiply across the herd.
2. Shutting down CAFO lagoons is key to stopping environmental gene transfer.
a. Resistant bacteria escape CAFOs through retail meat, farmworkers, and unlined manure lagoons that leach into groundwater and transfer resistance plasmids to human pathogens.
b. Cutting agricultural selection pressure and runoff preserves both global mortality prevention and routine hospital medicine.
D. Impact
1. Global mortality from antimicrobial resistance.

a. According to Murray and colleagues in 2022, in The Lancet, bacterial antimicrobial resistance directly caused 1.27 million deaths worldwide in 2019 and contributed to nearly 5 million deaths—exceeding HIV/AIDS or malaria.
2. Structural collapse of routine modern medicine.

a. Cesarean sections, cancer chemotherapy, organ transplants, and joint replacements depend on effective post-operative antibiotics; losing last-resort drugs turns routine surgery into a life-threatening risk.
ADVANTAGE 3: ENVIRONMENTAL RACISM (10/25/26)
A. Uniqueness
1. Industrial CAFO waste is concentrated in rural communities of color.
a. According to Wing and Johnston in 2014, industrial hog CAFOs in North Carolina are overwhelmingly and disproportionately sited near Black, Hispanic, and Native American communities.
2. Open-air lagoons store city-sized volumes of untreated waste.
a. A single large hog CAFO generates as much untreated fecal waste as a mid-sized city, stored in open-air pits and sprayed onto surrounding fields.
B. Link
1. The plan directly prohibits the CAFO facilities generating lagoon and sprayfield pollution.
a. Banning CAFOs nationwide shuts down the open-air manure lagoons and aerosolized waste spraying concentrated in the rural Black Belt.
2. Federal prohibition overrides state 'right-to-farm' shields.
a. State agricultural liability laws currently block rural residents from suing integrators over nuisance and toxic drift; a federal CAFO prohibition removes the offending facilities directly.
C. Internal Link
1. Ending open-air lagoon storage is key to stopping toxic air exposure.
a. CAFO lagoons and sprayfields volatilize ammonia, hydrogen sulfide, and particulate endotoxins directly into neighboring homes and schools.
2. Eliminating unlined waste pits is key to protecting rural drinking water.
a. Lagoon seepage and storm runoff leach nitrates and antibiotic-resistant pathogens into rural private wells, preventing ongoing environmental racism.
D. Impact
1. Ongoing structural respiratory and waterborne illness.
a. Residents living beside CAFOs suffer elevated rates of childhood asthma, acute respiratory distress, and contaminated drinking water every single day.
2. Proximate structural violence comes first on probability.
a. Ongoing daily harm to marginalized communities has a 100 percent probability and immediate timeframe, outweighing speculative economic adjustment costs.
SOLVENCY AND UNDERVIEW
1. Federal prohibition is necessary and sufficient to solve.
a. Enforcement operates directly through existing EPA Clean Water Act and USDA registries that already catalog CAFOs nationwide.
b. Only federal action stops the interstate race to the bottom, because single-state bans simply prompt integrators to relocate confinement barns across state lines.
2. Weigh consequences and probability first.
a. Even a marginal reduction in pandemic spillover or antibiotic resistance outweighs, because both harms are compounding, irreversible biological processes already underway.
b. Against any Kritik, outlawing CAFOs is a concrete material refusal of agribusiness confinement, and the permutation combines statutory prohibition with critical praxis outside the state.
